claims.text: Controlled slow cooling promotes targeted segregation of selected elements at high-entropy-alloy grain boundaries.
Selected grain-boundary elements influence intergranular cohesion.
Elemental segregation induced during slow cooling transforms straight grain boundaries into serrated grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary morphology governs toughness retention in high-entropy alloys.
Serrated grain boundaries distribute strain more evenly and reduce local strain concentrations.
Reduced local strain concentration inhibits intergranular crack initiation.
Serrated grain boundaries impede intergranular crack propagation.
Rapid cooling produces straight grain boundaries in the untreated baseline alloy.
Rapid cooling leaves the baseline grain boundaries unsegregated.
Straight baseline grain boundaries produce greater local strain concentration and facilitate intergranular cracking.
Straight-boundary, rapidly cooled material typically has lower toughness retention than the proposed slow-cooled material.
The tailored heat treatment will increase tensile fracture strain relative to a rapidly cooled control.
The tailored heat treatment will increase creep rupture life relative to a rapidly cooled control.
Approximately 650°C represents a demanding high-temperature engineering environment in which toughness retention is critical.
The proposed mechanism should hold for high-entropy alloys with similar compositions under high-stress, high-temperature loading near 650°C.
Changing alloy composition or processing outside the stated bounds may eliminate the serration-mediated toughness benefit.
Prior observations establish a correlation between serrated grain-boundary morphology and improved toughness.
